title: Will a 33-year-old walk-up apartment be hard to sell in 15 years?
excerpt: A buyer likes a first-floor freehold walk-up in Green Lane, Penang, near his parents, but worries about its age and resale. Sean explains walk-up pricing and the checks that matter.

question.asker: From A viewer who wrote in by email and asked to stay anonymous
question.context: The viewer is looking at a 1,000 sq ft first-floor unit in a 33-year-old freehold walk-up apartment in Green Lane, Penang, asking RM520,000. The established neighbourhood is central and quiet, the unit is well kept, parking is easy, and it is close to his parents' home. He would live there for about 15 years, and doesn't want a new launch because they are dense, small and far away.
question.text: Is an old walk-up apartment a sound buy, or will its age and low demand make it hard to sell later?

answer.quote: The only question is how much you want to sell.
answer.summary: It will sell in 15 years; the question is at what price, and nobody can promise a profit. Do the checks now: compare the asking price with other walk-ups and recent transactions nearby, get the bank's valuation, and look at the rents. Then negotiate with that data, and expect growth roughly in line with inflation.

reasons.title: In a walk-up, lower floors cost more
reasons.body: Without lifts, buildings stop at about five storeys, and the top floors are cheapest because of the stairs. The first floor is often the sweet spot: one flight of stairs, with a little more privacy than the ground floor.

reasons.title: Owner-occupiers keep a building in good shape
reasons.body: A building mostly lived in by its owners tends to be maintained by residents who care, unlike one full of investors' tenants. Check who lives there.

reasons.title: Data gives you room to negotiate
reasons.body: If similar units nearby ask RM500,000, he can use that to bring the price down. If the bank values the unit below the price, the difference must be paid in cash.

reasons.title: There will always be buyers like him
reasons.body: Some buyers will always prefer a quieter, lower-density walk-up to Penang's dense new blocks, as he does. Penang rents are lower than KL's, at about 2.5% to 3% of value, but higher rents still show demand.

actions: Compare the asking price with about 20 walk-ups and recent transactions in Green Lane.
Ask for the bank's valuation before agreeing a price.
Check rents for similar units nearby.
Find out whether most residents are owners or tenants.
Look up past transaction prices for Penang walk-ups to set realistic expectations.
caveat: Being freehold removes any concern about the lease. A new highway or rail line nearby could change the area's prospects either way, which no one can predict.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #190. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in October 2022.
